statement: A rope is folded in half. Then it is cut twice, straight across both layers, in two different places away from the fold. How many pieces of rope are there?

choices.misconception: I forgot about the fold and cut a straight rope in 2 places.
I counted the 4 places where the rope is cut, not the pieces.
I counted 2 pieces in each of the 3 parts of the folded rope, but the part with the fold is still one piece.
I thought each cut splits both layers into 2 pieces each, so each cut makes 4 pieces, and 4 + 4 = 8.

hints: Draw the rope opened out again after the cuts.
The folded rope has 2 layers, so each cut goes through the rope in 2 places. Draw the rope straight, mark every cut point, then count the pieces between and outside the marks.
Two cuts through 2 layers make 4 cut points on the straight rope. A rope with 4 cut points falls into the pieces between the marks plus the two end pieces.

solutions.reliable: The folded rope has 2 layers, so each cut goes through the rope in 2 places. Two cuts make 4 cut points. Opened out, a straight rope with 4 cut points splits into $4 + 1 = 5$ pieces. The middle one of these is the bent piece that went round the fold. The idea to keep: unfold the picture and count the cut points; on a single line, there is one more piece than cut points.
solutions.elegant: Look at the folded rope. The two cuts split it into 3 parts. The part with the fold is one bent piece, and each of the other 2 parts has 2 layers, so 2 pieces each: $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. The idea to keep: a piece that goes round a fold stays in one piece.

whyOnTest: Students cannot see inside the folded rope, so drawing it opened out is the only safe way to count the pieces.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
